title: Sex differences in the genetic basis of human recombination within 190,000 parent-child pairs
source: Biological sciences : Nature Communications subject feeds
abstract: Meiotic recombination drives genetic diversity and chromosome segregation, yet the genetic factors governing variation in human recombination rates across studies remain poorly understood. Here, we analyze 112,144 maternal and 78,653 paternal meiosis events across four countries and identify 58 independent genomic regions (24 unique across phenotypes) associated with recombination frequency and location. These include six novel female-specific regions harboring genes linked to ovarian function and a seventh novel region linked to male recombination, with many loci demonstrating sex-dependent effects. The between-sex genetic correlation is 0.374 (0.072 SD). While DNA markers account for 30-40% of individual-level variation in recombination rate, previously known global modulators explain only 37.7% (2.7% SD) of this variation in females and 47.1% (3.8% SD) in males. We create a polygenic predictor that significantly predicts recombination rates in women and men after adjusting for age and birth year. Furthermore, female recombination correlates significantly with reproductive outcomes and aging, after adjusting for study ascertainment. In the largest meta-analysis to date of human meiotic recombination, these findings uncover novel sex-specific loci and clarify the polygenic architecture underlying meiotic variation.

title: Humanized yeast ORC drives R-loop dependent transcription-replication conflicts and global gene dysregulation
source: Biological sciences : Nature Communications subject feeds
abstract: The Origin Recognition Complex (ORC) recruits Mini-Chromosome Maintenance (MCM) hexamers to initiate eukaryotic DNA replication. While yeast ORC binds specific DNA motifs, human ORC binds sequence-agnostically nucleosome-depleted promoter regions. Here, using a mutant yeast model that recapitulates the human ORC binding landscape, we demonstrate that pervasive and unscheduled ORC binding at promoters in the compact yeast genome generates R-loop associated transcription-replication conflicts and disrupts gene expression across thousands of genes. Unexpectedly, we also uncover that substituting endogenous gene promoters with a replication origin sequence maintains robust transcription. We reveal that this intrinsic, promoter-like function relies on the ability of origins to form a nucleosome-depleted region (NDR) encoded within the origin’s sequence composition. However, origin-substituted loci reposition the +1 nucleosome which drives the transcription machinery to select alternative transcription start sites (TSSs). Thus, origins and promoters share an intrinsic chromatin structure-controlled ability to drive transcription initiation. Together, our results show that origin licensing in compact genomes relies on sequence-specific, coupled origin licensing to insulate transcription from the replication machinery.

title: Sublevel-selective electron spin hyperpolarization of triplet radical pairs in metal–organic frameworks
source: Physical sciences : Nature Communications subject feeds
abstract: Molecular spin systems are promising platforms for spin-based technologies because their electronic structures can be synthetically tailored and integrated into higher-order assemblies. Photogenerated radical pairs can exhibit spin hyperpolarization under ambient conditions, yet extending such spin dynamics from isolated molecules to structurally organized materials remains challenging. Here, we report a metal–organic framework that regulates the generation of spin-polarized radical pairs within locally well-defined donor–acceptor arrangements. N,N’-di(4-pyridyl)−1,4,5,8-naphthalenetetracarboxdiimide is introduced into a zinc tetrakis(4-carboxyphenyl)porphyrin-based framework. Dense donor–acceptor packing promotes efficient quenching of the porphyrin singlet excited state and selectively forms strongly coupled triplet radical pairs polarized in the zero-spin projection sublevel. These radical pairs exhibit narrow electron paramagnetic resonance signals and long spin-lattice relaxation times. Their spin-lattice relaxation dynamics persist in various guest solvents and vary with guest identity, demonstrating a route to chemically responsive spin materials based on porous, locally organized donor–acceptor frameworks.

title: Strain-induced correlated metallic phase in 1T-TaS2
source: Physical sciences : Nature Communications subject feeds
abstract: Layered transition-metal dichalcogenide 1T-TaS2 has long been considered a prime example of a Mott insulator driven by strong electron correlations. However, this view has been recently challenged by proposals which favor a band insulating state arising from interlayer dimerization. This ongoing debate opens a frontier in 1T-TaS2 research focusing on stacking order, and raises a fundamental question with broad implications for two-dimensional materials: can electronic phases be engineered by actively tuning interlayer coupling? Here, using micro-focused angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy supported by first-principles calculations, we demonstrate that uniaxial strain drives 1T-TaS2 from its insulating charge-density-wave phase into a stable metallic phase. This metallic phase, distinct from hydrostatic-pressure-induced or non-equilibrium hidden phases, emerges via a strain-induced rearrangement in the interlayer stacking of the Star-of-David charge order, effectively disrupting interlayer dimerization. Furthermore, the emergent metallic phase exhibits a significant quasiparticle mass renormalization, a hallmark of strong electron correlations, indicating its correlated nature and proximity to a Mott instability. This finding necessitates a re-evaluation of the interplay between structural and strong correlations in 1T-TaS2. The present results establish uniaxial strain as a powerful method for tuning the interlayer coupling, opening pathways for exploring quantum phases inaccessible under ambient conditions.

title: Preadipocyte-Derived Decellularized Extracellular Matrix-Functionalized Three Dimensionally Printed Scaffolds Regulate Vascularized Adipose Tissue Regeneration via Modulation of Selected Paracrine Factors
source: ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract The clinical efficacy of soft tissue reconstruction is severely hindered by unpredictable graft resorption and inadequate vascularization. Traditional synthetic implant scaffolds offer mechanical support, with limited bioactivity for adipose tissue regeneration. In this study, we developed a “three-in-one” bioinstructive platform (dPCL) integrating structural support, signal induction, and immunomodulation by functionalizing a 3D-printed polycaprolactone (PCL) framework with a decellularized extracellular matrix (dECM) derived from 3T3-L1 preadipocytes. The obtained dECM-functionalized scaffold provided essential biochemical cues. In vitro assays demonstrated that dPCL significantly enhanced preadipocyte adhesion and adipogenic differentiation. Besides, the dECM-functionalized scaffold was found to modulate the secretion of selected paracrine factors, markedly upregulating the secretion of adiponectin, VEGF, and IL-10, which facilitated cell differentiation and robust endothelial network formation. In vivo evaluation in a murine subcutaneous model confirmed that dPCL scaffolds effectively supported the formation of stable, well-vascularized adipose tissue. Furthermore, the dECM-functionalized scaffold enhanced the recruitment and accumulation of proregenerative M2 macrophages, maintaining an M2-dominant tissue microenvironment that facilitated graft integration. In summary, current findings demonstrate that integrating cell-specific dECM with 3D-printed scaffolds creates a multifaceted bioactive platform that overcomes the critical barriers of vascularization and metabolic integration, presenting a highly promising strategy for functional soft tissue regeneration.

title: Interfacial Integration of Cross-Kingdom Membranes Establishes a Rechargeable Energy Cascade
source: ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Engineering modular adenosine triphosphate (ATP)-mediated energy transduction pathways from the bottom up faces two key bottlenecks: first, detergent-dependent reconstitution typically impairs protein activity and energetic coupling efficiency due to disrupted native lipid environments and randomized protein orientation; second, physically separated ATP production and consumption modules suffer from severe diffusional ATP losses and inefficient intermodule cascade coupling. To address both limitations, we report a programmable, nondestructive strategy to construct a high-performance artificial organelle—the “chrometabosome”—through orthogonal peptide-driven fusion of photosynthetic chromatophores and energy-consuming erythrosomes. Bypassing detergent solubilization and reconstitution, this strategy not only preserves membrane proteins in their native lipid environment and functional state but also colocalizes ATP-producing and ATP-consuming modules within a single nanoscale compartment. This colocalization reduces the dependence of ATP utilization on intervesicle transport, producing a 3- to 4-fold kinetic enhancement at lower vesicle concentrations relative to nonintegrated controls. This light-rechargeable system offers a modular framework for versatile biohybrid energy nanosystems.

title: Depth-enhanced molecular imaging with two-photon oblique plane microscopy
source: Biological sciences : Nature Communications subject feeds
abstract: High-numerical-aperture (NA) oblique plane microscopy enables noninvasive fluorescence imaging of subcellular dynamics without radical sample modification. However, performance degrades at depth in multicellular specimens as scattering and refractive-index heterogeneity raise out-of-focus background. We report a two-photon oblique plane microscope that improves resolution at depth by combining high-NA single-objective detection with multiphoton plane illumination. The microscope achieves ~ 300 nm lateral and ~ 650 nm axial resolution, with single-molecule sensitivity and 5 × faster volumetric acquisition (up to 3.25 × 106 voxels s−1). In multicellular contexts, near-infrared nonlinear excitation enhances contrast throughout the illumination depth by ~ 2 × and restores volumetric resolving power by > 2 × relative to linear excitation. We demonstrate these capabilities through molecular imaging of epithelial tissue, stem-cell-derived gastruloids, and living fruit fly embryos, including multicolor transcription-factor dynamics, optogenetic subcellular control, and single-mRNA tracking, all using standard glass-based mounting.

title: Vagal afferent activation induces a dissociated NREM sleep-like state with wake-related locus coeruleus activity
source: Biological sciences : Nature Communications subject feeds
abstract: Parasympathetic nervous system activity, vital for restorative sleep, is influenced by vagal sensory afferents, but how these shape brain-body correlates of sleep remains open. Here we combined vagal sensory neuron (VSN) stimulation in the mouse with EEG/EMG, heart rate, brain-body temperature, noradrenergic locus coeruleus (LC) neuron population activity measures and in vitro synaptic physiology to investigate the effects of VSN activation on sleep-wake states. We show that chemogenetic VSN stimulation during the resting phase induced a non-rapid-eye-movement sleep (NREMS)-like state with enriched, but homeostatically regulated, low-frequency (0.75–4 Hz) EEG activity, yet suppressed REMS. Simultaneously, brain-body temperatures dropped while LC activity increased. The gradual recovery towards normal NREMS-REMS-cycles was accelerated by external warming, identifying cooling as key contributing factor. We conclude that VSN activation can promote brain-body correlates as a continuum of normal NREMS while engaging wake-promoting forebrain neuromodulation, revealing a coexistence of classically incompatible sleep- and wake-associated signatures.

title: Thermodynamic-guided tailoring of single-atom coordination environments via oxygen chemical potential for efficient C-N coupling
source: Physical sciences : Nature Communications subject feeds
abstract: Systematic and precise regulation of coordination environments in single-atom catalysts (SACs) remains challenging due to thermodynamic constraints and kinetic traps. Herein, we report a thermodynamic-guided strategy to tailor the local coordination of Fe single atoms on CoWO4 support by regulating oxygen chemical potential. Via fine-tuning hydrogen partial pressure during pyrolysis, a series of Fe1Ox SACs is synthesized with well-defined Fe-O coordination numbers ranging from 3 to 6. Combining operando characterizations and density functional theory calculations, Fe1O4 is identified as the optimal configuration for hexamethylenetetramine (HMTA) electrosynthesis, which delivers balanced kinetics by moderating free water dissociation for *NH3 generation and strengthening HCHO chemisorption via pronounced Fe 3d-O 2p orbital hybridization near the Fermi level. As a result, the Fe1O4 SAC achieves a HMTA yield of 0.21 mmol h−1 cm−2 with 83.04% Faradaic efficiency at 1.75 V and stability over 200 h in a flow cell. This work establishes a universal thermodynamic approach for precise coordination engineering of single-atom electrocatalysts and provides a general paradigm for kinetically balancing complex multi-intermediate electrocatalytic systems.

title: Intrinsic neural dynamics reveal a body-part-specific topography in mouse secondary motor cortex
source: Biological sciences : Nature Communications subject feeds
abstract: The mammalian sensory cortex (S1) has a well-characterized body part-specific topography. However, most motor cortex atlases to date are only coarsely defined. Here, we demonstrate that optical mapping of neuronal activity in awake mice reveals a distinct, body-part specific organization of mouse secondary motor cortex (M2). This M2 topography was identified by recognizing that intrinsic neuronal fluctuations are selectively synchronized between homologous sub-regions of S1 and M2. These fluctuations were strongest during rest and quenched during movement, and were not prominent in corticospinal neurons (CSNs), indicating that they do not represent motor output. Functional characterization of M2 sub-regions during spontaneous movements confirms body-part specificity, and stronger engagement during multi-effector coordinated actions. Structural connectivity atlas tracings from S1 regions confirm projections to homologous M2 sub-regions. These results reveal an important underlying topography within M2, and demonstrate intrinsic neuronal dynamics as a window into the functional architecture of the motor cortex.

title: Comparative genomics analysis of luminescent and non-luminescent fireflies reveals mechanisms underlying adult light organs development
source: Biological sciences : Nature Communications subject feeds
abstract: The genetic and developmental basis for the gain and loss of complex traits remains a central question in evolutionary biology. We investigate the loss of the adult light organ (LO) in the diurnal non-luminous firefly Pristolycus diversecostatus as a natural case of lineage-specific gene loss. A high-quality genome assembly of Pri. diversecostatus, combined with comparative multi-omics and functional analyses with its luminous relative Aquatica leii, reveals that LO loss correlates with large-scale gene family contraction and transcriptional rewiring of three core metabolic modules. RNAi experiments in Aqu. leii show that Laccase2 is required for LO integrity and bioluminescence. Key regulators of LO-specific cuticle transparency are identified, and a homeobox centered gene regulatory network is uncovered. This multi-omics study provides a genome-wide perspective on the regulatory modules underlying a complex organ and offers a framework based on regulatory network simplification for understanding the formation and loss of complex traits in evolution.

title: miProbe: microbial peptide repository of biological embeddings
source: Biological sciences : Nature Communications subject feeds
abstract: Microbial peptides represent a vast yet largely underexplored component of microbial dark matter, offering a valuable reservoir of bioactive molecules. Artificial Intelligence (AI) has revolutionized peptide mining, demonstrating high-throughput screening capabilities in tasks such as functional prediction and de novo design. To fully unlock the potential of microbial resource, we present miProbe (https://www.biosino.org/iMAC/miProbe), an integrative platform hosting 1.08 × 109 microbial peptides from disparate habitats. Uniquely, miProbe bridges the gap between raw sequences and AI applications by providing 8 TB of precomputed protein language model embeddings (e.g., ESM2-650M and ProtT5-XL-U50). Our analysis reveals substantial variation in peptide diversity and functional properties across habitats and microbial taxonomic groups, and highlights the utility of large-scale embedding resources in functional peptide mining. Equipped with robust APIs for seamless model integration, miProbe establishes a diverse and scalable data resource to accelerate AI-driven exploration of microbial dark matter and the rational design of novel therapeutics.

title: A hierarchical metabolic flux orchestrates cell cycle transitions in bacteria
source: Biological sciences : Nature Communications subject feeds
abstract: Mechanisms interlinking metabolic cues with cell cycle programs remain unknown. We show that an oscillating cytosolic redox critically governs cell cycle transitions in Caulobacter crescentus. By integrating evolutionary genetics with metabolic flux tracing, we uncover temporally orchestrated shifts in core metabolic pathways that remodel cytosolic redox across the cell cycle. Early stages channel carbon flux toward unsaturated fatty-acid synthesis and a reverse-TCA to drive cytosolic oxidation-coupled G1-to-S transition. The later stages depend on an enhanced forward-TCA cycle that promote cytosolic reduction-driven proliferation. Strikingly, perturbing fatty-acid synthesis or reverse/forward-TCA cycle uncouples growth from proliferation. Intriguingly, a biphasic glucose uptake program dictates the cell cycle-stage-specific metabolism. These findings reveal a previously unrecognized metabolic-redox circuitry that coordinates cell cycle progression in bacteria. They further unveil several metabolic branchpoints as promising targets for chemical intervention to disrupt critical and conserved cell cycle events, with potential applicability to bacterial pathogens.

title: Directional motility of crystallizing cholesterol on supported lipid bilayers
source: Biological sciences : Nature Communications subject feeds
abstract: Cholesterol crystallization within phospholipid bilayers necessarily remodels the surrounding membrane, creating dynamic feedback between growing crystallites and locally changing membrane. Using fluorescence microscopy, we show that lipid-coated, cholesterol-rich crystallites self-propel on the bilayer surface along directional trajectories, including circular, unidirectional, and reciprocating motion. We hypothesize that crystallite motilities arise from local cholesterol depletion in the underlying bilayer, generating gradients in composition, rigidity, and thus adhesion, which induce directional forces analogous to those involved in haptotaxis and/or durotaxis. Fluorescence lifetime imaging with a mechanosensitive probe reveals time-resolved changes in membrane packing, consistent with this mechanism. Single particle tracking and mathematical modeling support the mechanical plausibility of a working model in which crystallization-induced cholesterol redistribution may generate dynamic rigidity gradients at crystallite–membrane interface. Tuning membrane states yields a quantitative operating map that relates composition to motility, providing model-dependent design guidance for controlling cholesterol crystallite transport on lipid interfaces.

title: LRH-1 coordinates metabolic and epigenetic programs that establish luteal cell identity
source: Biological sciences : Nature Communications subject feeds
abstract: Despite advances in assisted reproductive technology, success rates remain modest, largely due to implantation failure and inadequate support of early pregnancy. Corpus luteum function and consequent progesterone secretion are essential for these processes. Large luteal cells are the primary source of progesterone production, yet the transcriptional programs that define their identity remain unclear. Here, we identify the nuclear receptor Liver receptor homolog-1 as a key regulator of large luteal cell function. Loss of Liver receptor homolog-1 disrupts lipid droplet accumulation and downregulates key steroidogenic genes. Mechanistically, Liver receptor homolog-1 undergoes chromatin-binding reprogramming during luteinization, establishing regulatory regions that couple lipid metabolism to steroidogenesis. Large luteal cells integrate energy metabolism with steroid hormone production and promote nuclear acetyl-coenzyme A synthesis via Acyl-CoA synthetase short-chain family member 2, linking metabolic reprogramming to epigenetic control. These findings establish Liver receptor homolog-1 and Acyl-CoA synthetase short-chain family member 2 as key regulators coordinating lipid homeostasis, chromatin regulation and fertility.

title: Failure of TSPO-dependent metabolic compensation marks the loss of mitochondrial bioenergetic adaptation in parkin-deficient neurons
source: Biological sciences : Nature Communications subject feeds
abstract: Neurons require mitochondrial bioenergetic flexibility to withstand chronic mitochondrial quality control failure, yet the compensatory safeguards that preserve mitochondrial functional output during neurodegenerative progression remain unclear. Here, using parkin-deficient fly models, we identify an early mitochondrial metabolic signature characterized by reduced pyruvate and increased glutamate and α-ketoglutarate. Substrate-specific mitochondrial respiration and ATP assays showed impaired pyruvate-supported bioenergetic capacity but preserved glutamate-supported bioenergetic capacity, supporting a transient glutamate-linked compensatory state before neurodegenerative deterioration. We identify neuronal TSPO upregulation as an adaptive compensatory mechanism that sustains glutamate-supported mitochondrial bioenergetic capacity under parkin-deficient conditions. In human iPSC-derived neurons, parkin deficiency was similarly associated with TSPO upregulation, and TSPO modulation altered neuronal vulnerability. TSPO induction was controlled by JNK-Jun/Nrf2 signaling, whose age-associated attenuation compromised compensation and accelerated neurodegeneration. Thus, loss of TSPO-dependent glutamate-linked bioenergetic compensation marks the transition from mitochondrial adaptation to neurodegenerative deterioration under parkin-deficient conditions.

title: CCR8-depleting antibodies restore response to radiotherapy plus anti-PD1 therapy in head and neck cancer by targeting intratumoral CCR8+ regulatory T cells
source: Biological sciences : Nature Communications subject feeds
abstract: Despite advances in immunotherapy (IO) and radiation therapy (RT), anti-PD-1 (aPD-1) therapy has provided only modest benefit in head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC) for reasons that remain poorly understood. CCR8 is a chemokine receptor selectively enriched on tumor infiltrating regulatory T cells (Tregs), making it an attractive candidate for therapeutic targeting. Given our knowledge that immunosuppressive T-regulatory cells are associated with resistance to RT and IO, but have no effective targeting strategy in HNSCC, we investigate the depletion of tumor specific Treg subsets on tumor growth in female mice. In human and murine HNSCC, we characterize a subset of CCR8+ Tregs that are an immunosuppressive cell population associated with incomplete response to RT and IO. In preclinical models of HNSCC, we find that RT drives CCR8+ Treg infiltration into the primary tumor to promote tumor growth and recurrence, which can be reversed with administration of CCR8-depleting antibodies (aCCR8). Finally, we show that resistance to RT+aPD1 combination therapy is mediated by aPD1 activation of CCR8+ Tregs to facilitate tumor growth, which can be reversed with aCCR8. These findings reveal the immunosuppressive profile of CCR8+ Tregs in HNSCC and pave the way for novel combination strategies of IO in HNSCC.

title: Power-sensitive partnerships for just nature-based solutions in urban informal settlements
source: Scientific community and society : Nature Communications subject feeds
abstract: Nature-based solutions should better redistribute benefits and reduce climate risks for vulnerable groups in urban informal settlements. To enable this, we argue for power-sensitive partnerships and a deep commitment to pluralism in values, ways of knowing, and understandings of nature.

title: Dynamic chlorine vacancies enable X-ray-specific afterglow
source: Physical sciences : Nature Communications subject feeds
abstract: Afterglow luminescence in inorganic materials is conventionally attributed to pre-existing static defects that trap and gradually release charge carriers. However, the observation of afterglow activated only by specific types of excitation sources, such as X-ray-specific afterglow in certain phosphors, highlights an opportunity to move beyond this static trap model. Here we show that Bi3+ doped Cs2ZrCl6 crystals exhibit afterglow exclusively under X-ray excitation, with no such effect under ultraviolet illumination. We demonstrate that this behavior arises from the in-situ generation and self-healing of metastable chlorine vacancies (VCl) specifically driven by X-ray irradiation, directly correlating with afterglow kinetics. Advancing beyond previous vague attributions to Frenkel defects, our multimodal evidence unambiguously pinpoints VCl as the operative defect species. This discovery challenges the paradigm that afterglow requires static pre-existing traps, establishing a dynamic mechanism where metastable defects are created by the probing radiation and gradually disappear when radiation is removed. We further manipulate the afterglow kinetic through Sn4+ induced modulation of vacancy formation energy, extending the afterglow duration to multiple hours while maintaining a high light yield of 55670 photons MeV−1 and a low detection limit of 30.81 nGyair s−1. Finally, we integrate these crystals into a flexible PDMS composite film for X-ray imaging, achieving a high spatial resolution of 23.6 lp mm−1 that enables high-fidelity imaging of curved objects via time-resolved readout. Our findings open an avenue for designing smart scintillators with programmable, radiation-specific responses, with implications for flexible radiography and beyond.

title: Co-administration of the long-acting monoclonal antibody AZD7442 and bivalent Ancestral/BA.1 vaccination is well-tolerated in immunosuppressed patients highly vulnerable to infection with SARS-CoV-2 virus: the results of the multicentre, open-label, phase II randomised controlled, RAPID-PROTECTION trial
source: Biological sciences : Nature Communications subject feeds
abstract: Immunocompromised individuals remain at risk of severe COVID-19. This multicentre, open-label, phase II randomised controlled trial evaluated the safety, pharmacokinetics and immunogenicity of co-administering the long-acting monoclonal antibody AZD7442 with a bivalent (Ancestral/BA.1) mRNA/LNP SARS-CoV-2 vaccine. A total of 139 immunocompromised adults received AZD7442 followed 28 days later by vaccination. AZD7442 was well tolerated, with no serious adverse events. Serum AZD7442 concentrations peaked at day 28 and remained detectable across disease cohorts at day 180. Anti-Spike antibody responses increased after AZD7442 and reached their highest levels after vaccination. Although binding antibodies against Omicron variants increased post-vaccination, neutralisation of Omicron remained limited after both AZD7442 and vaccination. Vaccination preferentially boosted antibodies targeting S2, the S1 N-terminal domain and receptor-binding domain epitopes not bound by AZD7442, and increased S2-specific memory B cells. Vaccine-induced T-cell responses were cross-reactive between ancestral and Omicron variants. Our findings support consideration of combined antibody and vaccine strategies in future therapeutic antibody development. The trial is registered with the International Standard Randomised Controlled Trial Number registry (ISRCTN53507177).

title: Neuromelanin-inspired metal-selenomelanin nanonetworks restore neuronal excitability in radiation-induced brain injury
abstract: Radiation-induced brain injury (RIBI) affects up to 30% of patients receiving cranial radiotherapy, representing an irreversible complication lacking effective therapies. Research advances are limited by poor blood-brain barrier drug penetration and overreliance on ex vivo pathology, which cannot resolve dynamic neuronal dysfunction. Inspired by neuromelanin, we fabricated metal-selenomelanin nanonetworks (MSMNs), combined with in vivo electrophysiology to investigate and mitigate radiation-triggered neural dysfunction. In 6-gray whole body–irradiated mice, MSMN normalized neuronal excitability and restored medium spiny neuron firing and striatal circuit activity, improving locomotor and anxiety-related behaviors. Besides central functional recovery, MSMN provides systemic radioprotection, ensuring full 30-day survival, protecting radiosensitive organs and facilitating hematopoietic recovery. This work identifies neuronal excitability as an underexplored therapeutic target for RIBI, establishing neuromelanin-mimetic selenomelanin nanonetworks as a bioinspired platform linking molecular radioprotection to circuit-level restoration for radiation-induced neurological injury.

title: Transition-Metal-Catalyzed Multicomponent Cycloadditions
abstract: Abstract Transition-metal-catalyzed multicomponent cycloadditions provide a powerful strategy for constructing complex cyclic frameworks from simple unsaturated building blocks with high atom and step efficiencies. This Review highlights the progress made in transition-metal-catalyzed multicomponent cycloadditions based on the size of the cyclic products formed. First, reactions that construct five-membered rings, including [2 + 2 + 1], [3 + 1 + 1], and [2 + 1 + 1 + 1] cycloadditions, are discussed with an emphasis on key reactive intermediates, such as carbon monoxide, vinylidenes, carbenoids, and nitrenes. Next, six-membered-ring-forming processes, particularly [2 + 2 + 2], [3 + 2 + 1], [4 + 1 + 1], and [2 + 1 + 2 + 1] cycloadditions, are described, highlighting combinations of alkynes, alkenes, and heteroatom-containing components. The Review then covers strategies for constructing seven-membered rings via [3 + 2 + 2] and [4 + 2 + 1] cycloadditions. Finally, emerging methods that enable the formation of eight- and nine-membered rings through higher-order multicomponent cycloadditions are described. This Review aims to provide a comprehensive overview of the conceptual framework, mechanistic principles, and synthetic possibilities of transition-metal-catalyzed multicomponent cycloadditions by organizing them according to ring size and cycloaddition components.

title: A LiDAR-based reconstruction reveals increasing Arctic phytoplankton production during low-light winter-shoulder period
abstract:
Arctic marine productivity is traditionally considered concentrated in the sunlit season, yet low-light winter-shoulder periods remain poorly constrained because passive ocean color observations require sufficient solar illumination. Here, we use 2.39 million spaceborne LiDAR profiles from CALIOP (2006–2023) to reconstruct Arctic net primary production (NPP) and evaluate how active-sensor observations reduce this seasonal blind spot. The bio-optical retrieval model was trained using MODIS-constrained observations under illuminated conditions; accordingly, low-light estimates represent physically constrained extrapolations beyond the primary MODIS-observable training domain rather than direct NPP measurements. Within this framework, LiDAR increases winter half-year observational coverage from ∼20 to 30% to ∼70 to 75% and reveals widespread low-light winter-shoulder production across marginal seas and seasonal ice-edge regions. Pan-Arctic NPP integrated over this period increased at an estimated rate of 0.75 Tg C year
                    −1
                    during 2007–2023, whereas the corresponding passive-sensor signal was negligible. Accounting for this component raises annual Arctic NPP estimates by ∼13.3% indicating that passive sensor-based assessments may underrepresent the magnitude and seasonal structure of Arctic productivity. Associations with declining sea ice and surface warming suggest this underrepresented production is consistent with ongoing seasonal reorganization of Arctic carbon fixation. Uncertainties from model parameterization, low-light extrapolation, and limited in situ validation are largest in the lowest-light and highest-latitude regimes. These findings do not imply photosynthesis during absolute polar night, but show that active LiDAR observations with explicit light constraints and transparent extrapolation limits can test how unresolved low-light winter-shoulder production may alter Arctic NPP seasonality under continuing sea-ice loss.

title: Low-power Charge-domain In-FeRAM Computing
abstract: The growing energy demands of large-scale model training and scientific computing have inspired interest in low-power computing paradigms. In-memory computing (IMC) reduces data movement overheads, but resistive devices suffer from high static power and Joule-heating. Here, we introduce a charge-domain computing paradigm based on Hf0.5Zr0.5O2 ferroelectric random-access memory (HZO FeRAM), in which computation is enabled by linear accumulation of charge associated with the anti-orientated ferroelectric polarization. We experimentally demonstrate this concept using a 16-kbit HZO FeRAM array, where key computational characteristics execute directly within this array, gradient calculations are performed with errors below 6×10 − 3, and in-memory difference operations solve partial differential equations with 98% accuracy after only 21 iterations. Hybrid FeRAM-digital training of a single-layer neural network for letter recognition is also shown. Furthermore, a 1 μm2 HZO ferroelectric capacitor exhibits a measured switching energy of only 1.66×10 − 12 J, implying the potential of HZO FeRAM for energy-efficient charge-domain computing.

title: 2DIR hyperspectral imaging of polariton propagation reveals fewer dark modes per polariton
abstract: Change in chemical reactions under strong coupling with confined electromagnetic cavities has been previously experimentally observed. However, theoretically, the number of molecules per cavity mode is too high to explain the experiment. In this work, the authors experimentally measure this number, and find that it is much smaller than assumed, using 2DIR imaging and, thus, lay the foundation for better understanding polariton phenomena and future system design.

abstract: This work presents a dual-domain charge bootstrapping (DCB) strategy that decouples charge transport paths to extract energy from two electrostatically coupled charge domains for high charge accumulation and efficient energy utilization.

title: H-aggregated supramolecular packing lowers exciton binding energy for efficient quinone-phenol-mediated H2O2 photosynthesis
abstract: Controlling how molecules assemble provides a powerful route to regulate the fate of photoexcited states. H-type packing strengthens intermolecular electronic delocalization, weakens exciton binding, and promotes charge generation in perylene diimide (PDI) supramolecules, enabling efficient solar H2O2 photosynthesis. This work establishes supramolecular packing as a molecular design strategy for exciton management and solar-to-chemical energy conversion.

title: Donor–Acceptor Tuning Regulates Viologen Redox Behavior for Selective H2O2 Photosynthesis
source: ACS Energy Letters: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Regulating redox-active electron acceptors offers a strategy for directing multielectron photocatalysis beyond conventional charge-separation engineering. Here, we demonstrate substituent-controlled viologen redox regulation in pyrene–viologen porous organic polymers (PyVio-X) for selective H2O2 photosynthesis. Carbonyl functionalization (PyVio-CO) enhances donor–acceptor interactions and charge separation, while facilitating photoinduced viologen radical (V-N+•) formation. PyVio-CO achieves an H2O2 production rate of 1786 μmol g–1 h–1 in pure water under visible light and ambient air, with a solar-to-chemical conversion efficiency of 0.25% and an apparent quantum yield of 4.95%. Mechanistic investigations support sequential O2 reduction involving ·O2– and *OOH intermediates, mediated by reversible V-N2+/V-N+• redox cycling. Enhanced two-electron O2 reduction selectivity and suppressed H2O2 decomposition further promote H2O2 accumulation. This work establishes substituent-controlled redox mediation as a molecular design principle for selective multielectron photocatalysis.

title: Boosting stability and charge transfer of conducting polymer poly(benzodifurandione) (PBFDO) through complementary topology
abstract:
Poly(benzodifurandione) (PBFDO) is a benchmark n-type conjugated polymer known for its record-high electrical conductivity. Nevertheless, its thermal robustness and charge/ion transport characteristics remain insufficient. To address this issue, we report a hierarchical complementary topology strategy via doping PBFDO with choline chloride (ChCl). At the molecular scale, the cations Ch
                    +
                    selectively intercalate along the out-of-plane direction while simultaneously densifying the in-plane π-π stacking, accompanied by partial removal of H
                    +
                    . At the submicrometer scale, this induces distinct phase separation into high- and low-density stacking domains. As a result, the product PBFDO-ChCl exhibited a synergistic performance boost, with a 2.8-fold enhancement in high-temperature resilience, a 1.6-fold increase in sheet conductance, and a 15.9-fold reduction in ion diffusion resistance. Then, organic electrochemical transistors (OECTs) using PBFDO-ChCl as channel material further confirm these performance enhancements. As a whole, this work closes the performance gap between n-type PBFDO and state-of-the-art p-type conjugated polymers, potentially advancing its applications from energy storage to bioelectronics and neuromorphic computing.

title: Transition from Dehydration to Rehydration of Chloride Salts near the Melting Point: Thermodynamic Origin and Implications for High-Temperature Corrosion
source: ACS Energy Letters: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Molten chloride salts are promising functional media for high-temperature energy systems; however, trace water can accelerate corrosion of structural materials. We investigated changes in water concentration in six chloride salts—LiCl, NaCl, MgCl2, KCl, CaCl2, and ZnCl2—during heating across their solid-to-liquid phase transitions under a nominally inert Ar atmosphere. During solid-state heating, water concentration generally decreased, indicating dehydration. With further heating toward and through melting, however, this trend unexpectedly reversed in five salts except ZnCl2. As these salts entered the liquid phase, their water concentrations increased, marking a transition from dehydration to rehydration. Thermodynamic analysis showed that melting shifts the free energy balance toward water incorporation through enthalpic and entropic contributions. By comparing molten MgCl2 under conditions allowing or restricting entry of Ar gas, we identified trace water in the Ar atmosphere as the source of rehydration. Corrosion tests further showed rehydration substantially increased 316H stainless steel corrosion.

title: Evolutionarily reinforced GC-rich motif enables non-AUG translation in mammals under eIF1/5MP-mediated fidelity control
abstract:
Non-AUG translation contributes to proteome diversity, but its regulatory principles remain unclear. Here, we show that a GCC-rich upstream extension, termed the
                    NAT1
                    motif, acts as a potent enhancer of near-cognate initiation in mammals. Cell-free and reporter assays revealed that eIF1 and 5MP act as conserved inhibitors of non-AUG initiation across mammals and plants, while the
                    NAT1
                    motif enables enhanced initiation within this fidelity framework. Mutational analysis identified −6 and −7 positions within the GCC repeat as key determinants of motif activity. Genome-wide analyses uncovered evolutionary depletion of
                    NAT1
                    -type non-AUG codons in human 5′UTRs, suggesting purifying selection against excessive initiation. Nevertheless, more than a hundred retained sites are associated with genes involved in cell proliferation and migration, suggesting that regulated non-AUG initiation may contribute to disease-relevant translational programs. The motif’s enrichment within GCC repeats further suggests a mechanistic link to repeat-associated non-AUG translation.

title: Dynamics of excess renewable energy and implications for its potential use
abstract: Due to wind and solar variability, excess renewable energy could be available, even in systems with substantial storage. Across a wide range of possible systems, excesses typically occur in the afternoon and in spring and fall and persist for up to 7–12 h. Flexible technologies could be designed to utilize these excesses.

title: Declining environmental predictability erodes reproduction in a tropical seabird
abstract: Seasonal breeders often depend on predictable resource pulses, yet climate change may alter reliability without shifting average timing. Here, using satellite chlorophyll records and two decades of individual breeding data for a tropical seabird, we show that weakened breeding synchrony and declining and less consistent reproductive success were associated with increasingly variable bloom timing without a consistent directional shift. Focusing on average timing alone could mean that climate impacts on species are overlooked. The authors show that, for a tropical seabird model species, winter–spring phytoplankton blooms kept a stable mean timing but became more variable between years. Breeding synchrony weakened and reproductive success declined and became less consistent over the same two decades.

title: Photoenzymatic control of phosphorus radicals
abstract: Photoenzymatic catalysis has enabled an increasingly diverse range of asymmetric radical transformations, yet phosphorus-centred radicals have remained beyond its reach. Engineered enzymes now enable stereoselective hydrophosphinylation, including products bearing carbon stereocentres, phosphorus stereocentres, or both.

title: Tuning Mass Transport through Pressure Modulation for Lithium-Mediated Nitrogen Reduction
source: ACS Energy Letters: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Lithium-mediated nitrogen reduction (LiNRR) produces ammonia at ambient pressure and temperature, and gas diffusion electrodes (GDEs) have advanced its production rate by intensifying nitrogen availability. However, the mass transport of lithium, nitrogen, and proton donor within the GDE and how the balance of their fluxes governs LiNRR performance remain underexplored. Here, we spatiotemporally varied the balance of species fluxes in a LiNRR GDE by dynamically modulating the pressure difference across the electrode, which altered the position of the gas/electrolyte interface. We found that decoupling the pressures applied during the plating and resting steps of pulsed electrolysis leads to higher ammonia production rates compared to the corresponding static pressure conditions. Decoupled pressure modulation enables even lithium plating during electrolysis and fast transport of nitrogen and proton donor during subsequent ammonia formation steps. This strategy may unlock a new design space for LiNRR by dynamically optimizing the reaction interface.

title: Identification of gamma-hydroxybutyrate (GHB)–β-ribose as a promising biomarker enabling prolonged detection of GHB intake
source: AAAS: Science Advances: Table of Contents
abstract: For several years, forensic toxicologists have sought biomarkers to extend the detection window of gamma-hydroxybutyric acid (GHB), a drug suspected to be involved in drug-facilitated sexual assaults yet difficult to detect due to its rapid elimination, endogenous presence, and postsampling formation. In this study, we used samples from 30 participants in a double-blind, controlled trial, randomized to placebo or a single oral dose (50 milligrams per kilogram) of sodium oxybate, a GHB salt. We collected whole blood and urine samples over 5 days and used untargeted metabolomics to search for biomarkers. The most promising feature, previously suggested as a GHB-pentose, was identified as GHB-β-ribose by chemical synthesis and liquid chromatography–tandem mass spectrometry. Quantification showed elevated levels of GHB-β-ribose for up to 48 in blood and 24 hours in urine after GHB intake compared with endogenous levels in the placebo group and authentic forensic cases. Thus, we present GHB-β-ribose as a very promising biomarker for GHB intake, with the potential to extend the detection window for GHB.

title: When and how particles are removed by drops
source: AAAS: Science Advances: Table of Contents
abstract: Particulate contaminants decrease the power output of solar panels and the transparency of windows and are detrimental to microelectronics, where even a single particle can induce a short circuit. Despite substantial research on particle adhesion and self-cleaning, it remains unclear when and how a drop can remove a particle from a surface, thus efficiently cleaning the surface. Here, by combining lattice Boltzmann simulations and confocal microscopy experiments, we show that at least six different scenarios arise from the complex interplay between capillary and friction forces when a drop collides with a particle on a surface. Notably, the capillary force plays a dual role in particle removal: While its tangential component always drives removal, its normal component can also hinder it. We introduce a dimensionless capillary capture parameter that successfully predicts particle removal across a wide range of particle and surface properties. Our results reveal that the design of easy-to-clean surfaces should focus not only on maximizing hydrophobicity but also on minimizing the particle-surface friction.

title: Deep learning–assisted electron microscopy for apparent Z-height mapping of atomically dispersed catalysts
source: AAAS: Science Advances: Table of Contents
abstract: Atomically dispersed catalysts (ADCs) offer maximal metal utilization and local atomic/electronic structures, yet resolving their actual atomic configurations using aberration-corrected scanning transmission electron microscopy (AC-STEM) remains fundamentally constrained by depth ambiguity and complex experimental noise. Existing STEM–machine learning (ML) approaches often rely on ideal simulations or manual annotations, limiting their transferability to realistic ADC images and causing ambiguity between isolated atoms, projected dimers, and small clusters. Here, we develop a physics-informed, domain-adaptive CycleGAN-UNet framework for depth-aware ADC analysis. CycleGAN translates height-labeled simulations into experimental-like images while preserving atomic coordinates and apparent Z-height labels, and a depth-supervised UNet performs simultaneous atom localization and discrete Z-height classification. Support-specific simulations further incorporate support-dependent background contrast, including uniform amorphous carbon (am-C), am-C with local thickness variation, and crystalline supports, thereby improving the applicability of the framework to different ADC imaging conditions. Across diverse metals (Mn, Fe, Cu, Pd, and Pt) and supports (am-C, black phosphorus, and polymeric carbon nitride), the framework achieves high atom detection precision (∼95%) and reliable apparent Z-height classification at ∼2-nanometer binning. By encoding depth-dependent beam broadening features, the framework converts conventional 2D projections into quantitative, apparent Z-height atomic maps. In geminal Pt/PCN catalysts, it resolves the loading-dependent transition from isolated Pt monomers to Pt 2 sites and links these configurations to dehydrogenative aromatization activity. This framework transforms STEM images from projected atom maps into quantitative, depth-aware atomic descriptors for ADC structure–activity analysis.

title: ZSCAN4 links a transient reset of repetitive DNA to genome integrity and cellular plasticity
source: AAAS: Science Advances: Table of Contents
abstract: ZSCAN4 is transiently expressed in a small subset of embryonic stem cells and early embryos and has traditionally been linked to telomere elongation and genome stability. However, accumulating evidence indicates that ZSCAN4 does not function as a classical stemness factor. ZSCAN4 acts as a temporally restricted regulator of genome plasticity. Recent mechanistic studies indicate that ZSCAN4 preferentially operates at repetitive DNA regions. In particular, at telomeres, it supports maintenance and elongation, whereas, at microsatellite-rich and two-cell (2C)–associated loci, it has been proposed to enable a brief, locally restricted window of chromatin relaxation. This process involves noncanonical mechanisms, such as proteostasis-dependent removal of repressive chromatin complexes, coordinated engagement of genome surveillance pathways, and rapid restoration of chromatin constraint. ZSCAN4 activity is regulated by multilayered regulatory mechanisms acting at the transcriptional, posttranscriptional, and posttranslational levels, ensuring a sharp burst followed by active shutdown. We propose a unifying model in which ZSCAN4 functions as a transient genome reset factor that facilitates cellular plasticity during zygotic genome activation, 2C-like transitions, and cellular reprogramming, while preserving long-term genome integrity. This framework redefines the role of ZSCAN4 beyond stemness maintenance and highlights repetitive DNA as a central regulatory platform during developmental and reprogramming-associated genome transitions.

title: Symmetry as a common origin of hierarchical emergence and abstraction
source: AAAS: Science Advances: Table of Contents
abstract: Many systems of interest exhibit nested emergent layers with their own rules and regularities, and our knowledge about them seems naturally organized around these levels. How do such hierarchical structures arise, and why should observers track these hierarchies so closely? This paper proposes symmetry as an answer to both questions. By combining principles from information theory, group theory, and statistical mechanics, it is shown that dynamical processes that are equivariant with respect to a symmetry group give rise to multiple emergent macroscopic levels arranged according to the algebraic structure of the symmetry. The same symmetries shape the Bayesian beliefs of an observer with only partial access to the system, yielding a matching hierarchy of “abstract” beliefs that can be updated autonomously at different levels of resolution. These ideas are illustrated in Hopfield networks, where familiar macroscopic quantities emerge from known symmetries, and in Boolean models of gene regulation, where symmetries are instead found from the dynamics. The computational advantages provided by symmetry are showcased in Ehrenfest diffusion and epidemic modeling, where abstract beliefs enable Bayesian inference over exponentially large state spaces. These results identify symmetry as a sufficient mechanism for hierarchical emergence and—at the same time—for the capacity of abstract beliefs to mirror the systems they track, making feasible inferential problems that would otherwise be intractable.

title: Swarm-inspired magnetic metal-organic framework-based microbots for on-demand moisture manipulation
source: AAAS: Science Advances: Table of Contents
abstract: Hygroscopic metal-organic frameworks (MOFs) are promising candidates for atmospheric water harvesting (AWH) and humidity control. Nevertheless, their practical application is often hindered by the poor manipulability of inherent powder forms and mass transfer limitations caused by the shaping. Drawing inspiration from the “hot defensive ball” aggregation morphology of honeybee swarms, a versatile magnetic shaping strategy hereby was reported to assemble MOF-based microbots, which enhances the formability of MOF powders. The obtained magnetic hygroscopic MOF (mMOF-303) exhibits enhanced water adsorption kinetics and enables efficient regeneration via multimodal heating strategies, including photothermal, electrothermal, and magnetothermal heating. Besides, the magnetic MOF-based microbots can change their aggregation patterns and perform directional motion according to application scenarios, enabling rapid water vapor sorption-desorption rates and precision confined space humidity control. This work provides a universal strategy to impart versatile formability to static MOF powders, paving the way for MOF engineering and advanced moisture management.

title: Engineering exhaustion-resistance CD19 CAR T cells to address translational barriers for the treatment of cancer and autoimmune disease
source: AAAS: Science Advances: Table of Contents
abstract: PRGN-3008 is a CD19 CAR T cell designed to overcome key limitations in ex vivo and in vivo CAR T manufacturing, cost, safety, and therapeutic durability. Featuring decentralized overnight manufacturing without ex vivo expansion, PRGN-3008 is engineered using a single nonviral transposon to encode CD19 CAR, membrane-bound interleukin-15 (mbIL-15) for improved persistence, PD-1–targeting microRNAs to prevent exhaustion, and an inducible safety switch for controlled in vivo elimination. Safety studies showed low vector copy numbers, favorable integration profile, and efficient CAR T ablation upon safety-switch activation. The combined mbIL-15 expression and PD-1 down-regulation preserved PRGN-3008 polyfunctionality and sustained cytotoxicity across repeated tumor challenges, outperforming nonarmored or singly modified CAR T cells. In xenograft models, overnight-manufactured PRGN-3008 without ex vivo expansion and activation achieved durable tumor clearance, prolonged tumor-free survival, robust antigen dependent expansion, and enrichment of memory T cell phenotypes linked to clinical durability. Notably, PRGN-3008 generated from heavily pretreated patients with systemic lupus erythematosus or lupus nephritis, maintained effector function, resisted terminal differentiation under chronic antigen exposure, and effectively depleted autoreactive B cells in a humanized mouse model. Transcriptomic analysis revealed that the combination of mbIL-15 expression and PD-1 down-regulation enhances the expression of genes associated with bioenergetic pathways, including oxidative phosphorylation, mitochondrial biogenesis, glycolysis, and glutamine utilization, thereby supporting resistance to exhaustion and sustained effector function. Collectively, these data support PRGN-3008 as a clinically translatable, scalable, and controllable CAR T with the potential to expand access to cell therapy across oncology and autoimmune indications.

title: Raising mountains for a habitable Earth
source: AAAS: Science Advances: Table of Contents
abstract: The formation of mountain belts (orogens) elevates rocks above sea level, making them available for chemical weathering and altering the composition of the atmosphere and oceans, which in turn control habitability. Peak-metamorphic pressures recorded by crustal rocks buried in orogens increased between 2.7 to 2.2 and 0.8 to 0.7 billion years ago, indicating that rocks could be buried deeper and that orogens could grow substantially thicker after each of these periods. The two periods of orogenic growth were broadly synchronous with major increases in terrigenous element and nutrient fluxes and changes in biological sulfur metabolism and surface oxygenation. These changes could be explained by enhanced weathering of higher mountains. The findings support the hypothesis that there are first-order mechanistic links between secular geodynamic change and changes in Earth system state and habitability, which shaped the conditions for the evolution of complex life during the past 3 billion years.

title: GEX1-mediated semigamy induces both maternal and paternal haploids in cotton
source: AAAS: Science Advances: Table of Contents
abstract: How semigamy generates haploids during double fertilization has remained elusive for more than six decades. Here, we identify Gamete Expressed 1 ( GEX1 ) as the gene underlying semigamy and show that it mediates dual-origin haploid induction in cotton. A naturally occurring mutation in GEX1 disrupts normal nuclear membrane fusion during fertilization, resulting in delayed or incomplete karyogamy. Cytological analyses reveal that delayed karyogamy allows the closely apposed but unfused gametic nuclei to undergo independent mitotic divisions, giving rise to maternal haploids, paternal haploids, and chimeric progeny. CRISPR-Cas9–mediated disruption of GEX1 reproduced the characteristic defects in nuclear fusion and enabled both maternal and paternal haploid induction within a single generation. Together, our findings uncover a genetically tractable mechanism underlying semigamy that links nuclear membrane fusion dynamics to haploid formation and establish a versatile strategy for rapidly generating doubled haploids from both parental genomes to accelerate crop breeding.

title: Fault-tolerant quantum computing with high-rate symplectic double codes
source: AAAS: Science Advances: Table of Contents
abstract: High-rate and large-distance quantum codes are expected to make fault-tolerant quantum computing more efficient, but most of them lack efficient fault-tolerant encoded-state preparation methods. We propose such fault-tolerant encoders for two symplectic double codes, [[30,6,5]] and [[36,12,5]]. The advantage of these codes is their compactness, namely, their small code block sizes for their high encoding rates and large distance, allowing for early experimental realization of high-rate codes. Detecting crucial errors during encoding with as few auxiliary qubits as possible, our encoders can reduce resource overheads while keeping low logical error rates compared to more naive methods. Numerical simulations with a circuit-level noise model demonstrate the reliability and effectiveness of the proposed methods. We also develop arbitrary-state encoders that enable the injection of arbitrary quantum states into the code spaces. Combined with basic fault-tolerant operations, they support universal quantum computation. We thus demonstrate that efficient and reliable logical state preparation is achievable even for compact and high-rate codes, offering a potential step toward efficient fault-tolerant quantum computing suitable for near-term experiments.

title: Molecular thermal vibration assisted 1208-nm excitable photon upconversion with large anti-Stokes shifts
source: AAAS: Science Advances: Table of Contents
abstract: The anti-Stokes shift, a critical parameter reflecting the conversion of low-energy photons into high-energy photons, has been constrained by energy losses inherent to multi-step energy transfer processes. Here, we have demonstrated quantum dot–based photon upconversion under 1208-nanometer illumination (below the silicon bandgap, ∼1107 nanometer) and achieved unprecedented anti-Stokes shifts of 1.21 and 1.26 electron volt, which exceed the energy of a single excitation photon (1.03 electron volt). This breakthrough partially arose from the ideal energy cascade between quantum dots and ligands (NKU-0), coupled with nearly energy-lossless triplet fusion of the annihilators. Furthermore, we have found that the ground-state thermal vibrations of tetracene derivatives can promote the population of electrons to high vibrational states, which facilitated the endothermic triplet energy transfer from the ligand to the annihilator, thereby substantially enlarging the anti-Stokes shift. These findings present a feasible design route toward NIR-II–excitable photon upconversion with large anti-Stokes shifts by precisely tailoring quantum dot–based sensitizers and annihilator units, which promotes the efficient exploitation of low-energy photons in chemistry, materials science, and photonics.

title: The Azores plume origin of the New England Seamounts chain
source: AAAS: Science Advances: Table of Contents
abstract: Age-progressive seamount chains are fundamental archives in revealing the past plate motion and mantle convection. However, for a representative example such as the New England Seamounts chain on the North American Plate, both its plume source and its evolutionary trajectory remain debatable. This long-lasting uncertainty is mainly caused by the absence of quantitative high-resolution constraints on plume dynamics and its interactions with multiple plates. Here, we aim to answer this question using data-assimilation–based numerical simulations. We propose that the New England chain and the Corner Seamounts on the North American Plate, the Great Meteor Seamounts on the African Plate, and the Azores archipelago on the Eurasian Plate were created by a single plume—the Azores plume. This plume experienced two stages of motion through time. Subduction-induced sublithospheric mantle flow exerts a dominant control on the spatiotemporal distribution of volcanoes along the track and the geometry of this track, surpassing the influence of plume-plate interaction. The latter primarily affects the continuity of this trans-plate hotspot system. These findings offer a reinterpretation of hotspot-track formation and new constraints on how mantle flow reorganizes across multiple plates.

title: Increases in Northern Hemisphere winter circulation waviness over 1989 to 2011 driven by decadal oceanic variability
source: AAAS: Science Advances: Table of Contents
abstract: Large-scale circulation waviness shapes day-to-day weather and extremes. During 1989 to 2011, Northern Hemisphere midlatitudes experienced a pronounced increase in wintertime waviness, coinciding with rapid Arctic warming and more frequent cold-air outbreaks. While Arctic amplification was hypothesized to cause this trend via jet weakening, subsequent studies have failed to support this mechanism, leaving the origin unresolved. Here, using large-ensemble simulations, statistical analyses, and dynamical diagnostics, we demonstrate that variability in sea surface temperature and sea ice accounts for approximately half (48.7 to 63.3%) of the observed increase. A positive phase shift of the Atlantic Multidecadal Oscillation (AMO) is the prominent driver, enhancing waviness across northern Eurasia, the northwest Pacific, and the North Atlantic. A concurrent negative Interdecadal Pacific Oscillation shift partially offsets the AMO-driven anomalies in the northwest Pacific. Projections indicate that internal variability will outweigh model differences as the main source of near-term uncertainty. These results refine attribution of recent winter waviness changes and identify an AMO-linked source of predictability for long-term shifts in midlatitude extremes.

title: Lynx1 suppression reopens the window for effective rehabilitation after stroke in mice
source: AAAS: Science Advances: Table of Contents
abstract: Rehabilitation is an effective and reliable approach for promoting motor recovery after stroke. However, its efficacy decreases during the transition from the subacute to the chronic phase after stroke, posing a major barrier to complete functional recovery. This limited efficacy during the chronic phase is believed to result from declining neural plasticity. However, the molecular and cellular mechanisms regulating neural plasticity and its temporal changes after stroke remain unclear. To address this gap, we established a focal ischemic stroke mouse model that allows causal interrogation of the mechanisms responsible for the reduced efficacy of rehabilitation in the chronic phase. Using this model, we identified Lynx1, an endogenous negative allosteric modulator of nicotinic acetylcholine receptors, as a negative regulator of post-stroke neural plasticity. Lynx1 expression in layer 5 pyramidal neurons was transiently down-regulated and returned to normal levels in the peri-infarct area. Longitudinal intravital imaging revealed that Lynx1 suppression promoted synaptic clustering with increased dendritic spine turnover in the peri-infarct area, an emerging structural basis for memory formation. As anticipated, Lynx1 suppression improved spontaneous motor recovery and the efficacy of rehabilitation in the chronic phase after stroke. Furthermore, we developed a Lynx1 -targeting antisense oligonucleotide and found that its administration during the chronic phase after stroke enhanced the efficacy of rehabilitation. These findings suggest that dendritic spine dynamics in the peri-infarct area are a key determinant of rehabilitation responsiveness through the regulation of clustered spine formation and that Lynx1 may represent a promising therapeutic target for augmenting dendritic plasticity after stroke.

title: H3K9 demethylase KDM3A potentiates interferon signaling and macrophage-driven inflammation in atherosclerosis
source: AAAS: Science Advances: Table of Contents
abstract: Macrophages drive atherosclerosis through inflammatory activation programs shaped by metabolic and epigenetic reprogramming. H3K9 methylation enforces heterochromatin states and represses transcription, whereas removal of this histone modification creates transcriptionally permissive chromatin. Here, we identified KDM3A-mediated H3K9 demethylation to enhance chromatin accessibility at interferon (IFN) signaling loci, thereby promoting IFN production and downstream IFN-dependent transcriptional and chemokine responses. In a mouse model of atherosclerosis, hematopoietic Kdm3a deficiency reduces lesion size, necrotic core formation, and neutrophil recruitment. Mechanistically, Kdm3a -deficient macrophages show impaired chemokine secretion and reduced neutrophil recruitment both in vitro and in vivo. In primary human macrophages, KDM3A knockdown suppressed IFN responses; consistently KDM3A-dependent gene signatures were enriched in IFN-inducible macrophages within human atherosclerotic plaques, and computational modeling predicted a shift toward more stable plaque phenotypes upon KDM3A inhibition. Together, these findings establish KDM3A as an epigenetic regulator that sustains IFN-driven macrophage activation and promotes progression of atherosclerosis, nominating KDM3A as a potential target for selectively modulating IFN-dependent inflammation.

title: An end-to-end machine-learning system for global eddy-resolving ocean forecast
source: AAAS: Science Advances: Table of Contents
abstract: Machine learning (ML) models, especially those based on deep neural networks, have achieved competitive forecast accuracy and greatly reduced computational burden compared to traditional numerical global ocean forecast systems (GOFSs). However, it remains difficult for these ML models to operate on their own, as they rely on the initial conditions generated by numerical GOFSs. In this study, we present WenHai-E2E, an end-to-end ML GOFS that replaces the entire pipeline of numerical GOFSs at deployment time and makes eddy-resolving global ocean forecast directly from multisource heterogeneous ocean observations, without requiring operational initial conditions from numerical GOFSs. WenHai-E2E outperforms a state-of-the-art numerical GOFS in the forecast accuracy. Our results demonstrate the promise of ML GOFSs to surpass numerical GOFSs and provide insight into the pathway for developing next generation of GOFSs.

title: All-optical sensing of dermal activity enables an AI-powered wearable ring for continuous stress monitoring
source: AAAS: Science Advances: Table of Contents
abstract: Electrodermal activity (EDA), a primary stress-sensing signal in today’s wearables, requires skin-electrode contact that drifts and degrades over time, limiting long-term use. Here, we present an artificial intelligence (AI)–powered ring for all-optical sensing of dermal activity (ODA), using light rather than electrodes to track sweat gland activation, thereby enhancing durability and comfort. An optimized dual-wavelength design (960 and 1250 nanometers) captures perspiration dynamics while concurrently recording photoplethysmography. The ODA ring integrates temperature and motion sensors for multimodal monitoring with on-device inference. In correlation studies, ODA and EDA signals showed 86% agreement. In classification tasks, the ODA ring achieved 92.3% binary accuracy versus 77.95% for EDA. In multiclass tasks, ODA outperforms EDA by 100 to 74.58% (short term) and 89.72 to 43.20% (long term). On-device one-dimensional convolutional neural network inference enabled 87.53% autonomous accuracy. This electrode-free modality establishes a scalable, all-optical platform for rings, watches, and patches for accurate, robust, and long-term stress monitoring.

title: ChREBP drives diabetic kidney disease, and its inhibition confers renal protection
source: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences: Keyword search for query
abstract: Chronic kidney disease (CKD) represents a major medical burden. Diabetic kidney disease (DKD) is a leading cause of CKD, but intracellular pathways that can be pharmacologically targeted are poorly defined. Using transcriptome screening of DKD model mice we found that a carbohydrate-responsive element–binding protein (ChREBP)-dependent transcriptional cascade is markedly up-regulated in diabetic kidneys. Genetic ablation of ChREBP in diabetic mice ameliorated DKD, establishing ChREBP as a potential causal driver. A chemical screen based on ChREBP transcriptional activity identified D-532 as a small-molecule inhibitor that is effective in human and rodent cells. Oral administration of D-532 protected multiple diabetic mouse models from DKD progression and suppressed ChREBP and its downstream targets, including genes associated with excessive reactive oxygen species production. These findings position ChREBP as a pharmacologically targetable transcriptional driver of DKD and provide proof of concept that ChREBP inhibition can confer renal protection.

title: People know who to ask for favors despite underestimating compliance
source: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences: Keyword search for query
abstract:
Whether and how people approach social interactions hinges on how they expect others to respond. Extensive social psychology research suggests that people are inaccurate interpersonal perceivers, overestimating negative responses (e.g., discomfort) and underestimating positive responses (e.g., appreciation) across a variety of social situations. However, this conclusion is based almost exclusively on mean-level bias analyses that obscure the dyadic nature of interpersonal judgment and rely on a narrow conceptualization of interpersonal accuracy. Leveraging research on favor-asking and anticipated compliance as an exemplar, we demonstrate that interpersonal accuracy takes multiple theoretically distinct forms, and that the prevailing conclusion that people misunderstand their influence over others—because they tend to underestimate compliance—is likely overgeneralized. Across four studies (13,196 directed dyadic ratings), we show that people accurately differentiate between
                    who
                    will comply with
                    their
                    favor requests (dyadic meta-accuracy) despite the average tendency to underestimate compliance (mean-level bias). This pattern emerged for specific and general favor requests, among well- and newly-acquainted individuals, and beyond what could be expected due to self-projection. Through this dyadic lens, people are highly adept judges of their influence over others, as they are able to target their requests toward individuals who are uniquely likely to acquiesce to them—and can avoid wasting time on those who are not. Thus, our research refines existing implications for how people approach asking for favors. More broadly, by aligning theory, measurement, and level of analysis, our studies elucidate the need for greater theoretical precision and empirical breadth in interpersonal accuracy research.

title: Aneuploidy impairs B cell development but accelerates their MYC-driven transformation
source: AAAS: Science Advances: Table of Contents
abstract: Chromosomal instability (CIN) is an established driver of aneuploidy and cell death. Here, we investigate the role of apoptosis as a barrier against CIN-driven aneuploidy in B lymphocytes. We found that impairment of their spindle assembly checkpoint via deletion of Mitotic Arrest Deficient 2-Like 1 or mutation of Monopolar Spindle 1 kinase curtails B cell survival. A CRISPR screen identified intermediates of mitochondrial apoptosis as critical, which we confirmed in vivo by overexpression of a B cell–restricted BCL2 transgene, outperforming loss of P53 . Notably, cell death inhibition by BCL2 was insufficient to cause aneuploidy-driven B cell transformation, while loss of P53 strongly synergized with tumors featuring stochastic aneuploidies. In contrast, high cell death rates rapidly select for specific karyotypes, facilitating aneuploid tumor cell survival in E μ -Myc transgenic mice. Hence, cell death inhibition fails to allow CIN-driven aneuploidies to prevail. In contrast, BCL2-regulated apoptosis selects viable aneuploid tumor karyotypes in the presence of oncogenic MYC, a notion with implications for the clinical use of BCL2-targeting therapies.

title: Two-phase NEUROD1 pioneer activity synchronizes sensory neuronal differentiation and subtype specification
source: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences: Keyword search for query
abstract:
Temporal control of neuronal differentiation is essential for establishing stable neuronal identities, yet the transcriptional and epigenetic mechanisms underlying this process remain poorly understood. Using auditory neurons as an in vivo model, we investigate the role of the proneural factor NEUROD1 in regulating neuronal differentiation timing and subtype specification. To bypass early neuronal loss in germline
                    Neurod1
                    deletion mutants, we generated a delayed, self-terminating conditional knockout mouse (
                    Neurod1ST
                    ) that permits analysis of later differentiation stages. Integration of NEUROD1 chromatin binding and histone profiling at embryonic day (E) 11.5 with transcriptomic analyses across E11.5, E14.5, and E18.5 reveals a two-phase regulatory program during auditory neuron development that parallels dynamic
                    Neurod1
                    expression. In the first phase, coinciding with
                    Neurod1
                    upregulation during early neuronal differentiation, NEUROD1 preferentially binds putative enhancers of neuronal differentiation genes and promotes their transition to active chromatin states, consistent with pioneer factor activity. Loss of
                    Neurod1
                    disrupts these epigenomic transitions, resulting in persistence of progenitor-like states with premature activation of differentiation and axonogenesis programs. This dysregulation is accompanied by activation of alternative regulatory networks, leading to defective neuronal migration and innervation, progressive identity instability, and apoptosis. In the second phase, marked by reexpression of
                    Neurod1
                    in developing Type Ib/Ic precursors,
                    Neurod1
                    deletion selectively impairs Type Ic specification while promoting a Type Ib-like identity. These findings identify NEUROD1 as a temporal regulator that coordinates developmental progression and stabilizes auditory neuron identity through phased regulatory activity, providing a mechanistic framework for how pioneer transcription factors couple chromatin remodeling to developmental timing.

title: Structural and biochemical insight into allosteric regulation of the human 2-aminoadipic semialdehyde synthase
source: AAAS: Science Advances: Table of Contents
abstract: Multiple clinically relevant inborn errors of metabolism occur in lysine degradation, yet the regulation of this biochemical pathway remains poorly understood. The initial rate-limiting step of lysine catabolism is catalyzed by the bifunctional enzyme 2-aminoadipic semialdehyde synthase (AASS). Here, we report the cryo-EM structure of the full-length 400-kilodalton tetrameric AASS enzyme complex with substrates and products bound to both the lysine-2-oxoglutarate (LOR) and saccharopine dehydrogenase (SDH) catalytic domains. We also identified allosteric compounds that modulate the activity of AASS by reacting with cysteine-414 and shifting the pH optimum for biochemical activity. The mutagenesis of this allosteric Cys 414 has marked effects on the enzyme’s conformation and activity despite being more than 12 angstrom from the active site. We find that small changes near the hinge of an enzyme can have large effects on its catalytic properties. Last, targeting allosteric cysteines may be a general strategy for modulating enzyme activity by altering the dynamics of the enzyme.

title: Electrical spin pumping in exchange-coupled molecules
source: AAAS: Science Advances: Table of Contents
abstract: Electron spins in single molecules are a promising platform for quantum information processing. However, their practical implementation as qubits requires reliable control at the single-entity level, including an efficient state initialization. Here, we demonstrate the remote, all-electrical spin pumping of the electron spin in single molecules: Using electron spin resonance scanning tunneling microscopy, we investigate coupled pairs of S = 1/2 molecules, where one molecule serves as a readout and pumping unit for the neighboring one. We show that the exchange interaction between them enables angular momentum transfer, which allows for the control of the remote spin state via the direction and magnitude of the spin-polarized tunneling current and the exchange coupling strength.
